content: A sebaceous cyst is a closed sac located beneath the skin that contains a cheese-like or oily material. The primary symptom of a sebaceous cyst is typically a small, painless lump under the skin. However, if the cyst becomes infected or inflamed, additional symptoms may develop, including redness of the skin, tenderness or soreness in the affected area, and warmth over the site of the cyst. In some cases, a grayish-white, cheesy, and foul-smelling material may drain from the cyst. Sebaceous cysts most commonly develop as a result of swollen hair follicles. Skin trauma can also trigger the formation of these cysts. The process involves the creation of a sac of cells that secretes a protein called keratin. These cysts are most frequently found on the face, neck, and trunk. They are generally slow-growing, painless, and freely movable lumps beneath the skin. However, in certain cases, the cyst may become inflamed and tender. In most instances, a physician can diagnose a sebaceous cyst by visually examining the skin. Occasionally, a biopsy may be required to exclude other potential conditions. It is important to contact a healthcare provider if you notice any new growths on your body. While sebaceous cysts are not inherently dangerous, a medical professional should evaluate them to rule out the possibility of skin cancer. Treatment for sebaceous cysts is often unnecessary, as they are not harmful. Applying a warm, moist compress to the area may encourage the cyst to drain and heal. For small, inflamed cysts, a doctor may administer a steroid injection to reduce swelling. If the cyst becomes significantly swollen, tender, or large, a physician may opt to drain it or surgically remove it. Large or painful cysts can sometimes interfere with daily activities. In rare cases, sebaceous cysts may become infected, leading to the formation of painful abscesses. Additionally, there is a possibility that the cyst may recur even after surgical removal.
